objectives: Recognize recurring -it and -in patterns in taught short /i/ words.
Compare changing initial consonants while preserving the shared ending.
Apply word-family knowledge without replacing full decoding.
concepts: Word families share recurring sound-spelling endings.
The onset can change while the rime stays stable.
Pattern recognition supports automaticity but every grapheme still needs checking.

definitions.definition: A group of words sharing a common ending sound-spelling pattern.
The vowel and following sounds in a syllable, such as -it or -in.
Reading text that mainly uses previously taught sound-spelling patterns.

workedExamples: sit and pit share -it but have different initial consonants.
pin and tin share -in but have different initial consonants.
Even when -in is familiar, decode the complete word.
commonMistakes: Skipping full decoding because the family looks familiar.
keyTakeaways: Use families to support, not replace, decoding.
revisionPoints: Shared rime + changing onset = word family.

basic: Sort taught words into -it and -in families.
conceptual: Identify shared ending and changing onset.
higherOrderThinking: Explain why word-family recognition should not become guessing.
mixedReview: Sort, decode and read controlled sentences.

mistakeBasedRevision: If a familiar ending leads to a wrong word, return to full decoding.
weakTopicRevision: Read each word sound by sound, then reread the family.

outcomes: Learner sorts short /i/ words into -it and -in families with at least 80% accuracy.
Learner identifies shared rime and changing onset.
Learner reads family words accurately without guessing.
Learner answers simple controlled-text questions with at least 80% accuracy.

questions.question: Which word belongs to the -it family?
Which word belongs to the -in family?
What stays the same in pin and tin?
What changes between pin and tin?
Why are word families useful?
options: They remove the need to read

questions.question: When reading a familiar word family, what should the learner still do?
options: Check all graphemes and blend the word

questions.question: Which word does NOT belong with sit and pit?
Which word does NOT belong with pin and tin?
Read: “Tim sat at a mat.” Where did Tim sit?
What is the goal of this lesson?
options: Recognize short /i/ word families while maintaining accurate controlled reading
